To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the friction of hydrogen-terminated diamond counterfaces sliding on amorphous hydrogen-free carbon films decreases with increasing load and that this decrease is associated with the formation of tribochemical products.

1) the average friction in sliding contacts of hydrogenated diamond (111) with diamond (111)-like amorphous carbon films is independent of film thickness, 2) the average friction increases with increasing degree of counterface hydrogenation, and 3) the average friction is independent of the potential energy function used, indicating that long-range interactions do not contribute significantly to friction.
The atomic-scale frictional properties of amorphous hydrogen-free carbon films depend on film thickness and on the adhesion between the film and the diamond substrate."

the tribological properties of amorphous, carbon-based coatings.
the development of a new class of materials, amorphous carbon, for tribological applications.
the atomic-scale friction, and the effect of film thickness and film structure, of diamond (111) sliding against hydrogen-terminated diamond surfaces coated with amorous carbon.

the frictional behavior of amorphous, hydrocarbon-free carbon films in contact with hydrogen-terminated diamond counterfaces is governed by a complex combination of factors, including the film thickness, adhesional forces, and long-range forces.
the friction is dominated by the short-range forces and that the long-range forces are important, but not dominant.
the friction is determined by the film structure, adhesion, long-range forces, and the sliding speed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the average friction is dominated by short-range interactions.
friction is a function of the film thickness, the degree of adhesion, and the long-range interactions.
friction is primarily a surface phenomenon, but long-range forces can play a role in determining the magnitude of friction and wear.

the long-range interactions have a significant impact on the magnitude of the friction, and that the friction is sensitive to the degree of saturation of the counterfaces.
friction and wear in amorphous carbon films can be controlled by varying film thickness, the adhesion between the counterface and the film, and by the long-range interactions.
